Build daily living, self-care, and school-readiness skills

Help caregivers practice strategies across everyday routines

Behavior technicians provide direct therapy under BCBA supervision.

aba.title: ABA Services
aba.intro: Applied Behavior Analysis uses positive techniques and principles to bring about meaningful and positive change in behavior.

topics.title: What is Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA)?
paragraphs: Considered by many experts the gold standard therapy for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and other developmental conditions among children, ABA focuses on gradually improving social, communication, and daily living skills using positive reinforcement.
VTCC has experienced autism specialists in Virginia who use an evidence-based approach to improve functional, social capacity, and quality of life for children and families.

topics.title: Where can ABA be used?
paragraphs: These techniques can be used in structured situations such as at home, during family meals, or at a neighborhood playground.
Some ABA sessions involve one-on-one interaction between the therapist and the child. Group instruction can also be useful.

topics.title: How is ABA therapy provided to children with ASD or developmental disorders?
paragraphs: ABA therapy provides comprehensive, individualized, and intensive early intervention programs for children with autism. These interventions are designed to begin before the age of 4 and address a full range of life skills, from communication and sociability to self-care and school readiness.
Programs often range from 20–40 hours per week for 1–3 years, depending on clinical recommendation and authorization.

topics.title: How successful is ABA as an approach?
paragraphs: Research and academic literature indicate ABA is one of the most effective tools available to assist children with ASD. It is a joint effort between therapists and parents to stabilize behaviors associated with ASD by reinforcing positive behaviors, strengthening communication and social skills, and training parents to communicate effectively with their children.

ABA aims to reduce symptoms, improve skills and ability, and maximize the child's function and participation in the community. It is a widely accepted treatment approach among healthcare professionals and is used globally.

ABA is tailored to the specific needs of the child based on analysis of the family and physical environment and its effects on the child's behaviors. The focus of ABA remains on improving social and communication skills and on training parents in effective management of behaviors associated with ASD. Participation and a strong alliance between parents and therapists play a crucial role in reaching milestones.

topics.title: What is the process of receiving ABA services from VTCC?
items: A Board-Certified Behavior Analyst (BCBA) assesses the child to determine needs, define treatment goals, and identify beneficial milestones.
Parents provide additional information about the child's abilities and areas that are difficult for them.
Based on assessment, review of reports, and parent input, the BCBA develops the treatment plan and sets initial and terminal goals.
Goals incrementally increase the skills the child needs to learn and help them function to the best of their ability.
To decrease interfering behaviors, the BCBA develops a behavior intervention plan for the child.
One or more technicians then provide treatment to the child under the supervision and direction of the BCBA.
The BCBA monitors progress across the child's goals.

topics.title: What are some basic ABA philosophies followed at VTCC?
items: The analyst meets regularly with family members and program staff to plan, review progress, and make adjustments as needed.
Parents and other family members and caregivers receive training so they can support learning and skill practice throughout the day.
The child's day is structured to provide many opportunities—both planned and naturally occurring—to acquire and practice skills in structured and unstructured situations.
The child receives abundant positive reinforcement for demonstrating useful skills and socially appropriate behaviors. The emphasis is on positive social interactions and enjoyable learning.
The child receives no reinforcement for behaviors that pose harm or prevent learning.

topics.title: What kind of progress can be expected with ABA?
paragraphs: The aim of ABA is to give the child the ability to communicate effectively and to fully function within their environment. Interventions are tailored to achieve maximum progress. Every child improves at a different pace depending on the skill areas involved.
Consistent, repeated, and intensive effort—and partnership with parents—often leads to the best outcomes from therapy.

topics.title: Who can provide ABA services to my child or the child I am referring?
paragraphs: In most cases, a therapist or behavior technician (BT) trained and supervised by a BCBA will provide direct therapy to your child.
The BCBA holds a post-graduate degree in psychology or behavior analysis, is certified through a national board certification exam, and holds a state license to provide treatment.

categories.title: What Is ABA Therapy?
categories.intro: Applied Behavior Analysis uses positive, individualized strategies to help children build skills that support learning, communication, and daily life.

faqs.question: What is ABA therapy?
faqs.answer: ABA is an evidence-based approach that focuses on teaching meaningful skills and reducing behaviors that interfere with learning, safety, or daily routines. Treatment plans are individualized and adjusted as the child progresses.

faqs.question: Who may benefit from ABA?
faqs.answer: ABA is often used for children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder or related developmental needs, but every plan depends on assessment, clinical recommendation, funding, and family goals.

faqs.question: What happens during a typical ABA session?
faqs.answer: Sessions may include structured teaching, play-based learning, communication practice, daily living routines, and caregiver coaching. Activities depend on the child's treatment plan and current goals.

faqs.question: How is progress measured?
faqs.answer: The clinical team tracks progress toward specific goals over time. Plans are reviewed regularly so strategies can be updated as skills improve or new needs emerge.

faqs.question: How long does ABA last?
faqs.answer: Length of services varies by child, funding authorization, and clinical need. Some families receive support for months, while others may continue longer depending on goals and plan approval.

faqs.question: Is ABA only for young children?
faqs.answer: No. ABA can support a wide age range depending on clinical need, funding, and service authorization. VTCC can help families understand whether ABA may be appropriate for their child.

categories.title: What To Expect During Intake
categories.intro: Intake is the process of gathering information, reviewing funding, and determining whether VTCC services are a fit.

faqs.question: How do I start the intake process?
faqs.answer: Call VTCC or submit the request form on this site. A team member can help identify the service you need, explain paperwork, and outline funding review steps.

faqs.question: What information should I have ready?
faqs.answer: It helps to have parent or guardian contact information, the child's age, the service you are requesting, your city or county, and basic funding details such as Medicaid, MCO, commercial insurance, or county/FAPT information if known.

faqs.question: What forms may be required?
faqs.answer: Required forms depend on the service and funding source. Download the intake and referral forms from the Forms & Downloads page, or contact VTCC if you are unsure which documents apply.

faqs.question: How long does intake take?
faqs.answer: Timelines vary. Some steps move quickly after contact, while funding verification, authorization, and scheduling may take longer depending on the payer or referral source.

faqs.question: What happens after I reach out?
faqs.answer: VTCC reviews your request, confirms service and funding fit when possible, and guides you through paperwork, verification, assessment scheduling, and treatment planning.

faqs.question: What if I am not sure which service I need?
faqs.answer: That is common. Contact VTCC and describe your concerns. The team can help determine whether ABA, Early Learners, the Feeding Program, the Social Skills Group, or another pathway should be explored.

categories.title: Medicaid and FAPT Funding Basics
categories.intro: Coverage questions can be confusing. These answers explain common funding pathways families and referrers ask about most often.

faqs.question: Does VTCC accept Medicaid?
faqs.answer: VTCC's public materials reference Medicaid and managed care options. Families should contact VTCC to confirm current participation for their specific plan and service.

faqs.question: What is an MCO?
faqs.answer: A managed care organization, or MCO, administers Medicaid benefits for many Virginia families. Coverage and authorization rules may differ by plan and service type.

faqs.question: What is FAPT or county funding?
faqs.answer: Some families may access services through county or FAPT-related funding pathways. Eligibility, required documents, and approval steps vary by locality and service.

faqs.question: How do I verify my coverage?
faqs.answer: Have your insurance or funding information ready when you contact VTCC. The team can help identify what may be needed before services begin, though final approval depends on the payer or funding agency.

faqs.question: What if my plan is not listed on the website?
faqs.answer: Plan participation can change. Contact VTCC directly to ask whether your current plan or funding source may be accepted for the service you need.

faqs.question: Does commercial insurance cover these services?
faqs.answer: Commercial coverage depends on the plan, service type, and authorization requirements. VTCC can help families understand what questions to ask, but the insurance plan makes the final coverage decision.

categories.title: Parent Training FAQs
categories.intro: Parents and caregivers are essential partners in both ABA and family-centered services.

faqs.question: Why is parent training part of ABA?
faqs.answer: Children practice skills across daily routines at home, school, and in the community. Parent training helps caregivers use strategies consistently when therapists are not present.

faqs.question: Do I need to be present during every session?
faqs.answer: Participation expectations vary by treatment plan and funding requirements. VTCC can explain what involvement is recommended for your family.

faqs.question: What if more than one caregiver supports the child?
faqs.answer: Multiple caregivers can participate when appropriate. The clinical team may provide guidance so routines stay consistent across parents, grandparents, or other supports.

faqs.question: Can parent training help between sessions?
faqs.answer: Yes. Training often focuses on everyday moments such as transitions, communication, meals, bedtime, and community outings.

faqs.question: What if English is not my first language?
faqs.answer: VTCC was founded to support multicultural families. Ask the team about language support, translated materials, and communication options during intake.

faqs.question: What if I feel overwhelmed as a caregiver?
faqs.answer: Many families feel that way when starting services. Parent training is designed to offer practical strategies and support, not to add pressure. Tell your team what feels manageable.

categories.title: Referrals and Eligibility
categories.intro: Schools, doctors, case managers, county partners, and families can all start the conversation with VTCC.

faqs.question: Who can refer to VTCC?
faqs.answer: Families, schools, pediatricians, therapists, case managers, county partners, and other community professionals may contact VTCC to ask about services and referral requirements.

faqs.question: What information should referrers include?
faqs.answer: Helpful details often include the child's age, parent or guardian contact information, service requested, reason for referral, funding source if known, and any required referral paperwork.

faqs.question: Can families refer themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. A parent or guardian can contact VTCC directly to ask about services, intake steps, and funding review.

faqs.question: How should documents be sent?
faqs.answer: Use only the contact methods VTCC provides for referral and intake documents. Do not send sensitive records through an unsecured form or email unless VTCC has approved a secure process.

faqs.question: How quickly will VTCC respond?
faqs.answer: Response times vary by urgency, completeness of information, and office workload. If there is an immediate safety emergency, call 911.

faqs.question: Can VTCC tell me if a child is eligible before I refer?
faqs.answer: VTCC can often discuss general service fit and required next steps, but final eligibility may depend on funding authorization, clinical assessment, and documentation.

categories.title: Early Learners Program
categories.intro: The Early Learners program helps preschool-aged children practice skills for school and social settings.

faqs.question: What is the Early Learners program?
faqs.answer: It is a program for preschool-aged children focused on communication, play, routines, early learning, and participation in school and social settings.

faqs.question: What skills may children practice?
faqs.answer: Goals may include transitions, following directions, communication, play, social engagement, early learning, and independence. Goals are individualized for each child.

faqs.question: How are caregivers involved?
faqs.answer: Caregivers collaborate with the team so children can practice useful skills across everyday routines and prepare for settings outside the program.

categories.title: Feeding Program
categories.intro: The Feeding Program uses ABA practices and positive support to help children expand food repertoire and preferences.

faqs.question: What does the Feeding Program do?
faqs.answer: The program supports children as they practice accepting and exploring a wider variety of foods, tastes, textures, and presentations.

faqs.question: How are feeding goals chosen?
faqs.answer: Goals are individualized around the child’s current eating patterns, family priorities, and response to gradual practice and positive reinforcement.

faqs.question: Are caregivers included?
faqs.answer: Yes. Caregiver collaboration helps connect program goals with practical mealtime routines at home.

categories.title: Social Skills Group
categories.intro: The Social Skills Group gives clients who are ready for advanced practice a supported setting to learn with peers.

faqs.question: Who may be a fit for the group?
faqs.answer: The group is for clients who are ready to work on more advanced social skills and who may benefit from supported practice with peers.

faqs.question: What skills may the group address?
faqs.answer: Topics may include sarcasm, humor, conversation, flexible thinking, joining activities, problem-solving, and age-appropriate peer play.

faqs.question: How are group goals individualized?
faqs.answer: Staff provide coaching and feedback while each client works toward goals that match their current skills and social priorities.

structure.title: Clear clinical roles, from technician to analyst
structure.intro: ABA cases are designed by a Board Certified Behavior Analyst and carried out by trained technicians under that supervision. Specialized programs sit alongside that clinical structure. Titles below describe how care is organized—not a published org chart or headcount.

roles.title: Behavior Technician (BT)
roles.body: BTs provide most day-to-day ABA sessions. They implement the treatment plan, collect data, and practice skills with the child under a BCBA's direction. Many BTs complete VTCC's RBT training pathway while they work.

roles.title: Senior Lead Behavior Technician (SLBT)
roles.body: SLBTs are experienced technicians who take on higher-level clinical help: assessment support, new-hire training, side-by-side coaching, Safety-Care instruction, and Initial Home checklist interviews.

roles.title: Student Analyst
roles.body: RBTs enrolled in a qualifying master's program who accrue BACB restricted and unrestricted fieldwork hours on the job, under a qualified supervisor and a signed fieldwork contract.

roles.title: Board Certified Behavior Analyst (BCBA)
roles.body: BCBAs assess needs, write treatment and behavior-support plans, supervise technicians, train caregivers, and monitor progress. Independent practice in Virginia also requires state licensure.

roles.title: Specialized program clinicians
roles.level: Early Learners, Feeding, and Social Skills
roles.body: Clinicians in VTCC’s specialized programs support early learning, feeding, and social-skills work under the same culturally responsive, family-centered approach.

roles.title: Office and operations support
roles.body: VTCC's public career form also accepts interest in office administrative roles and internships that keep scheduling, intake, and clinic operations running.

differentiator.eyebrow: How VTCC differs from many ABA clinics
differentiator.title: We run the RBT training program in-house
differentiator.body: A common hiring path in ABA is to send new technicians to a third-party 40-hour course and an outside assessor. VTCC conducts the RBT training program itself. New Behavior Technicians complete the 40-hour RBT credentialing coursework here, VTCC conducts the competency assessment in-house, and the RBT exam is taken at a Pearson VUE / Pearson Professional Center.

steps.title: 40-hour RBT coursework
steps.body: Training includes the 40-hour Registered Behavior Technician credentialing curriculum that meets BACB training requirements. The BACB does not itself teach this course; employers, universities, or approved trainers deliver it. VTCC provides that coursework as part of employment training.

steps.title: In-house competency assessment
steps.body: After coursework, a qualified assessor at VTCC conducts the initial RBT competency assessment. The assessment checks that the technician can perform required tasks competently before they apply to the BACB.

steps.title: Exam at Pearson VUE
steps.body: The RBT examination is administered by Pearson VUE at a Pearson Professional Center or other authorized Pearson VUE site. VTCC does not administer the exam. After BACB application approval, the candidate schedules the computer-based exam through Pearson.

bt.title: Behavior Technician (BT)
bt.meta: Full-time, part-time, and internship interest · Fairfax, Virginia
bt.summary: Behavior Technicians provide direct ABA therapy under BCBA supervision. This is VTCC's primary clinical hiring role and the usual entry point into the RBT pathway.

youWill.title: What you will do
items: Implement skill-acquisition and behavior-support plans written by the BCBA
Collect session data so the clinical team can review progress
Practice communication, daily-living, play, and safer replacement skills with the child
Work in homes and other natural settings, and at the clinic when a case is scheduled there
Share observations with the supervising BCBA and follow the treatment plan as written
Partner with caregivers during sessions so strategies can be used in daily routines

training.title: Training and RBT credentialing
training.body: VTCC's Behavior Technician training includes the 40-hour RBT credentialing coursework. After that coursework, the company conducts the initial competency assessment in-house. The RBT exam is taken at a Pearson VUE / Pearson center—not at the clinic. Certification still depends on BACB eligibility, application approval, and the exam. VTCC's role is to provide the coursework, the in-house competency assessment, and supervised practice.

requirements.title: What this role asks of you
items: A genuine interest in working with children, adolescents, and families
Reliability for scheduled sessions and clear communication with supervisors
Willingness to complete VTCC's 40-hour RBT coursework and in-house competency assessment
Comfort implementing written plans and collecting data under BCBA supervision
Ability to meet BACB RBT eligibility rules if you pursue certification (including any education and background or abuse-registry checks the BACB or Virginia requires)
requirements.note: VTCC's public career form also lists Qualified Behavior Technician (QBT) as an interest option. Some technicians begin direct work while they complete RBT credentialing.

bcba.title: Board Certified Behavior Analyst (BCBA)
bcba.meta: Supervisory clinical role · Virginia practice requires state licensure
bcba.summary: BCBAs lead ABA assessment, treatment planning, technician supervision, and caregiver training. This section lists the education, certification, and licensing baseline for practicing as a behavior analyst in Virginia.

education.title: Minimum education
education.body: Applicants need a graduate degree that meets current Behavior Analyst Certification Board (BACB) degree requirements. In practice that is typically a master's degree in behavior analysis, education, psychology, or a related field, plus the required graduate coursework in behavior analysis. Coursework and degree rules are set by the BACB and can change; candidates should confirm current requirements on bacb.com before applying.

certification.title: BACB certification
certification.body: Independent work in this role requires current Board Certified Behavior Analyst (BCBA) certification from the BACB. Certification is earned by completing the required degree and coursework, accruing supervised fieldwork, and passing the BCBA examination. VTCC expects BCBAs to practice under the BACB Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts.

licensing.title: Virginia licensing
licensing.body: Virginia law requires a license to practice as a behavior analyst. The Virginia Board of Medicine issues the Licensed Behavior Analyst (LBA) credential to people who hold current BCBA certification and meet the Board's application rules. Candidates who are not yet licensed in Virginia should be eligible to obtain the LBA before practicing independently. Holding a BCBA certificate alone is not a license to practice in Virginia.

youWill.title: What you will do
items: Assess children and write individualized treatment and behavior-support plans
Supervise Behavior Technicians and review session data
Train parents and caregivers so skills can be practiced across daily routines
Adjust goals as the child progresses and as authorizations allow
Support Student Analysts who are accruing restricted and unrestricted fieldwork hours
Uphold ethical, culturally responsive care for diverse Northern Virginia families

otherOpenings.title: Other ways people apply
otherOpenings.body: The current VTCC career form also accepts interest in office administrative staff roles and internships, and in full-time or part-time schedules. Use the application page to tell us which path you are asking about. This page does not invent openings that are not already represented on the public career form or in the programs described here.

programs.title: Support after you are hired
programs.intro: These programs sit alongside day-to-day case work. They are written to match how the terms are used in ABA practice. Details of schedules, pay, and enrollment are confirmed with the clinical team after hire.

items.title: Student Analyst Program
items.summary: Graduate fieldwork while you work as an RBT
items.body: The Student Analyst Program is for RBTs who are enrolled in a master's program that can lead toward BCBA (or related) certification. On the job, those staff accrue BACB supervised fieldwork hours—not just a second job title.
details: Restricted hours are time spent delivering therapeutic and instructional procedures directly to clients. Much of ordinary RBT session work falls here. Restricted hours may count toward fieldwork when they meet BACB rules, but they cannot make up the majority of a BCBA trainee's accepted hours.

Unrestricted hours are analyst-level work: observing and analyzing data, helping design programs, training staff or caregivers, contributing to assessments, and other tasks that resemble what a BCBA does. BACB rules require a substantial share of fieldwork to be unrestricted—currently at least 60% for BCBA trainees.

Hours only count when a qualified supervisor, a signed fieldwork contract, monthly contacts and observations, and BACB documentation are in place. Routine RBT work does not automatically become fieldwork.

items.title: Monthly RBT PDUs
items.summary: Continued education, training, and clinical quality
items.body: Professional Development Units (PDUs) are employer-sponsored learning hours. VTCC's monthly RBT PDUs are continued education for technicians: skill refreshers, ethics and documentation, treatment integrity, and other clinical-quality topics.
details: These sessions are about staying sharp on the job and raising the quality of care—not a substitute for BACB certification itself.

RBT recertification with the BACB is a separate process (including supervision and a competency assessment). Monthly PDUs support clinical quality and professional growth; they should not be described as official BACB continuing-education units unless a given session is later approved as such.
Attendance expectations and topics are set by the clinical team.

items.title: Senior Lead Behavior Technician (SLBT)
items.summary: Higher-level clinical help from experienced technicians
items.body: The SLBT role is a senior technician track. SLBTs still provide excellent direct care, and they also take on structured leadership tasks that keep cases and new staff moving.
details: Assessment support: assisting BCBAs with portions of assessment activities that a trained senior technician can carry out under direction.
New-hire trainers: teaching recently hired BTs how VTCC runs sessions, collects data, and communicates with families and supervisors.
Shadowing BTs: joining sessions to give hands-on assistance and side-by-side training when a technician needs coaching.

Safety-Care trainers: delivering Safety-Care, a crisis-prevention and safety curriculum used so staff can prevent and respond to unsafe behavior with approved strategies. Trainers teach colleagues; they do not replace clinical or emergency protocols.

Initial Home checklist interviews: structured conversations that walk through the home-start checklist before a case begins—setting, materials, safety considerations, and caregiver contacts—so the first sessions are prepared.

recognition.title: Employee of the Month and Grounds for Greatness
recognition.intro: VTCC recognizes people who show up for families and for each other. Names and photos of current honorees are published only when leadership approves them. The programs themselves are described here so applicants know recognition is part of clinic life.

items.title: Employee of the Month
items.body: A monthly honor for a staff member whose work stood out—clinical quality, reliability with families, teamwork, or culturally responsive care. It is a formal, time-bound recognition, not a job title or a change in credentials.

items.title: Grounds for Greatness
items.body: Shoutouts for specific moments of excellence: a well-run session, support for a new hire, careful documentation, or a kindness that made a hard day easier. Grounds for Greatness is meant to catch everyday work that might otherwise go unseen, alongside the monthly honor.

feedingProgram.intro: The Feeding Program uses ABA practices to help children expand their food repertoire and preferences through individualized goals, positive support, and gradual practice.

Individualized goals and positive reinforcement
Caregiver collaboration during everyday meals
Progress monitoring and adjustments based on the child’s response

Back-and-forth conversation and flexible thinking
Age-appropriate peer play and shared activities
Joining groups, solving problems, and repairing misunderstandings

Coaching and positive feedback from trained staff
Opportunities to practice skills in realistic interactions
Family collaboration to support carryover beyond the group

hero.headline: ABA Therapy Designed Around Each Child
hero.body: Applied Behavior Analysis is an evidence-based approach that uses positive strategies to help children build meaningful skills. VTCC creates individualized ABA plans based on assessment, family input, and each child's strengths and needs.

sections.title: What ABA Can Support
items: Communication
Social interaction
Daily living routines
School readiness
Play and leisure skills
Emotional and behavioral regulation
Safer replacement behaviors
Caregiver-supported skill practice at home
sections.note: Every child is different. VTCC designs goals based on assessment, observation, caregiver input, and clinical recommendations.

sections.title: How VTCC Provides ABA
steps: A Board Certified Behavior Analyst reviews the child's needs.
The family shares information about strengths, challenges, routines, and priorities.
The BCBA creates treatment goals and a behavior support plan when appropriate.
Behavior technicians or therapists may provide direct services under BCBA supervision.
Parents and caregivers receive guidance so skills can be practiced across daily routines.
Progress is monitored and plans are updated as the child grows.

sections.title: Parent Training
sections.body: Parents and caregivers are essential partners in ABA therapy. VTCC supports families with strategies they can use during everyday routines, transitions, communication moments, and challenging situations.

cta.body: Not sure if ABA is the right fit? Contact VTCC and our team can explain the intake process, funding requirements, and next steps.

hero.headline: Insurance And Funding Guidance
hero.body: Understanding coverage can be confusing. VTCC helps families and referral partners review available funding pathways and identify what information may be needed before services begin.

sections.title: Funding Pathways
sections.body: VTCC's current public website references Medicaid, managed care organizations, commercial plans, and county/FAPT funding. Before this page is published, leadership should confirm the exact accepted plans and funding requirements for each service.

sections.title: Verification Process
items: Child's full name and date of birth
Parent or guardian contact information
Insurance card or funding source
Service being requested
Referral documents, if required
Diagnosis or clinical documentation only if requested through an approved secure process

sections.title: Important Note
sections.body: Coverage and eligibility vary by service, plan, authorization requirements, and funding source. VTCC can help verify information, but final coverage decisions may depend on the insurance plan, managed care organization, or funding agency.

hero.headline: Refer A Child Or Family To VTCC
hero.body: VTCC welcomes appropriate referrals from families, schools, pediatricians, therapists, case managers, county partners, and community professionals.

sections.title: Referral Information To Include
sections.intro: To help VTCC respond efficiently, referrers may be asked for:
items: Child or adolescent's name and age
Parent or guardian contact information
Service requested
Reason for referral
Funding source or insurance information
Relevant referral paperwork
Urgency or safety concerns, if applicable
sections.note: Do not send sensitive documents through an unsecured form or email unless VTCC has provided an approved secure method.

cta.body: Questions about eligibility or referral fit? Contact VTCC before sending documents.

hero.headline: Resources For Families And Referral Partners
hero.body: VTCC offers educational resources to help families understand ABA therapy, the Early Learners program, the Feeding Program, the Social Skills Group, parent involvement, intake steps, and funding questions.

faqs.question: What services does VTCC provide?
faqs.answer: VTCC provides ABA therapy, an Early Learners program, a Feeding Program, and a Social Skills Group for children and families. Services depend on eligibility, funding, clinical need, and availability.

faqs.question: What is the Early Learners program?
faqs.answer: The Early Learners program is for preschool-aged children and focuses on building communication, play, routines, and early learning skills that help children participate in school and social settings.

faqs.question: What does the Feeding Program support?
faqs.answer: The Feeding Program uses ABA practices to help children gradually expand their food repertoire and preferences through individualized goals, positive support, and caregiver collaboration.

faqs.question: Who may be a fit for the Social Skills Group?
faqs.answer: The Social Skills Group is for clients who are ready to practice more advanced social skills, such as understanding sarcasm, navigating conversation, and participating in age-appropriate peer play.

faqs.question: Where does VTCC provide services?
faqs.answer: Services may be provided through individualized and group settings based on the program, treatment plan, and availability. Contact VTCC to confirm current service options for your location.

faqs.question: Does VTCC accept insurance?
faqs.answer: The current site lists several Medicaid, managed care, and commercial payers, and also references county/FAPT funding. Families should contact VTCC to verify current coverage for their plan and service.

faqs.question: What is ABA therapy?
faqs.answer: ABA is an evidence-based approach that uses positive strategies to help children build skills and reduce behaviors that interfere with learning, safety, or daily life.

faqs.question: Do parents participate?
faqs.answer: Yes. Parent and caregiver involvement is an important part of individualized services and helps children practice skills across daily routines.

faqs.question: How do I get started?
faqs.answer: Call VTCC or complete the request form. The team can explain which program may fit, required forms, funding review, intake, assessment, and scheduling.

faqs.question: Can professionals refer a child?
faqs.answer: Yes. Schools, doctors, case managers, county partners, and other professionals can contact VTCC to ask about referral requirements.
